title: Etta's Mirror Maze Surprise
markdown:
The town fair smelled of sweet candy, and the games played happy music. The whole place buzzed. A balloon man lost a balloon and then found it again, which Etta wrote down as interesting. Etta, a curious girl with sparkling eyes and a little notebook always ready, walked with Moss the hedgehog, whose happy rumble was like a warm hug and who always had a plump berry to share. Nana Bea guided them, lavender-scented, kind at explaining, and she bought three tickets before anyone could argue about the price of wonder.

Whizz, bang, pop went the rides. Laughter bounced off a hoop-toss stall and came back almost like an echo, which Etta noted for later. A child won a wooden fish and immediately looked for another. Etta’s eyes twinkled like fireflies. “Look! The mirror maze!” A tent shimmered with colourful lights, the entrance flap slapping as if it were clapping them in.

They stepped inside. A world made of Etta — more Ettas than you could count. Waving. Peeking. Looking right back. All smiling, some taller because the glass bent, some chopped off at the knees. Moss scurried close to Nana Bea’s sensible shoes, nose twitching, berry clutched like a compass that had stopped working. “So many Ettas!” His voice wobbled like a tiny bell rung too hard. One extra Moss appeared in a corner and then proved to be only shine.

“They’re just reflections,” Bea said, calm as a stream. She left the dear-Moss off.

Etta tilted her head. Why so many? Fun, and a puzzle. She raised her right hand. The Etta in the glass raised her left. A backward picture. A tickle in her brain. She tiptoed closer and poked a smooth shiny surface. The reflection poked back. Her explorer brain whirred. These were not real Ettas. Pictures of light on shiny glass. Copies of every move, mixed-up.

“I’ve figured it out.” Eyes round as coins. “The mirrors show us ourselves, a backward copy. Like a puddle, but standing up.” She held up her right hand again. The reflection held up its left. Moss’s little heart thumped. Bea beamed. “You’ve observed it.”

“If we see a path that looks like it goes that way” — she pointed at a shimmering walkway in the glass — “we actually walk this way.” Opposite. A secret code, if you liked that sort of talk.

Etta led, explorer boots soft on the floor. Look at a reflection, then point the real way. “This way!” Once she almost trusted a glittering corridor that ended in her own waving hand; she stopped, checked the opposite, and found scuffed floorboards instead of shine. Bea and Moss followed her understanding, not the mirrored paths. They weaved and ducked, giggling at dozens of shiny selves, always choosing the solid real path. Moss tried to chase his reflection and bumped his nose gently on the glass. “Oops. Reflections can’t be chased.” He sat down to recover his dignity, berry still unshared.

Just as they thought they might be circling, a bright welcoming light peeked through. The exit.

“Hooray!” Moss did a hedgehog wiggle.

Bea scooped Etta into a hug. She named it once: reflections. Backward copies. Like the bathroom mirror when you brush — right hand on the left side of the glass. No speech about wonders hiding in plain sight.

Etta’s notebook was already open. “A puzzle made of light.” Pencil dancing. They stepped into the fair’s sunshine. She closed the book on the last page so the next maze, if there was one, would have somewhere to start. Moss offered the plump berry at last, which had waited politely through all the extra Ettas.
